**Truth — Ballad of Good Counsel** *(a polished rendering)*

Flee from the throng, and dwell with steadfast truth;
Content yourself with what you own, though small.
For hoarding breeds but hatred, climbing danger,
The crowd knows envy, and prosperity blinds all.
Desire no more than what your need requires;
Govern yourself well, you who counsel others,
And truth shall set you free—of this have no doubt.

Do not torment yourself to right all wrongs,
Trusting in Fortune, who turns as does a ball.
Great peace resides in little busy striving;
Beware, therefore, lest you should kick against an awl,
And strive not as the earthen pot against the wall.
Master yourself, who seek to master others' deeds,
And truth shall set you free—of this have no doubt.

Receive with humble grace what is bestowed on you;
The wrestling for this world invites a fall.
Here is no home; here lies but wilderness.
Go forth, O pilgrim! Forth, poor beast, out of your stall!
Know your true country! Look aloft! Give thanks to God for all!
Hold to the noble path, and let your spirit lead you,
And truth shall set you free—of this have no doubt.

Therefore, O Vache, forsake your old-time wretchedness;
Cease now to be the world's enslavèd thrall.
Cry mercy of Him who, in His lofty goodness,
Made you from nothing; and, above all,
Draw close to Him, and pray, in general,
For your own soul and others', that heavenly reward,
And truth shall set you free—of this have no doubt.

---

Escape from the crowds and make your home with honesty; be content with what you own, however little it may be. Storing up wealth breeds hatred, and ambition brings instability; the crowd is full of envy, and prosperity blinds everyone completely. Desire no more than what you truly require; govern yourself well if you presume to advise others—and honesty will set you free, of that there is no doubt.

Do not torment yourself trying to straighten everything that is crooked, relying on Fortune, who spins like a rolling ball. Great contentment lies in keeping your affairs simple; therefore take care not to kick against a sharp point, and don't quarrel the way an earthen pot battles a stone wall. Master your own nature, you who wish to control the deeds of others—and honesty will set you free, of that there is no doubt.

Accept whatever comes to you with patient obedience; struggling for worldly gain only invites a downfall. This place is no true home—it is merely a wilderness. Move on, pilgrim, move on! Go forth, beast, out of your stall! Recognize your true homeland! Lift your eyes! Give thanks to God for everything! Keep to the high road, and let your spirit guide you—and honesty will set you free, of that there is no doubt.

And so, you Vache, abandon your old misery; give up now being enslaved to the world. Beg for mercy from Him who, out of His supreme goodness, created you from nothing, and especially turn toward Him, praying both for yourself and for others as well, to gain the reward of heaven—and honesty will set you free, of that there is no doubt.

# On Living a Contented and Virtuous Life

There is great wisdom in fleeing the relentless pressures of worldly life and finding contentment in what one already possesses, however modest those possessions may be. A life lived in truthfulness, free from constant striving and discontent, offers a peace that no amount of accumulated wealth can provide. To be satisfied with one's own lot is not a sign of weakness or lack of ambition, but rather a mark of genuine wisdom.

Indeed, excessive greed, unbridled ambition, and the ceaseless pursuit of prosperity yield nothing but bitter fruit. Those who chase after ever-greater wealth and status often find themselves surrounded by hatred, plagued by instability, and consumed by envy—both their own and that of others. Moderation, by contrast, proves to be the far wiser path, granting stability and inner calm to those who embrace it.

We must also recognize the limits of our own power. Rather than exhausting ourselves in the impossible task of correcting every wrong in the world, or waging futile battles against forces far stronger than ourselves, we would do better to focus on what lies genuinely within our control: our own conduct. The mastery of oneself is a nobler and more attainable victory than any attempt to reshape the whole world according to our will.

For we must remember that this world is not our true home. It is merely a temporary wilderness through which we pass—a place of trial and transience rather than permanence. Understanding this, a person should lift their eyes upward, keeping in mind their heavenly destination and allowing their spirit, rather than fleeting earthly desires, to guide their steps.

Finally, let us abandon the old wretchedness that has weighed us down, and cease being enslaved to worldly things that can never truly satisfy. Instead, let us turn to God in humble prayer, seeking divine mercy and trusting in the reward that awaits those who order their lives toward what is eternal.

# Truth: Chaucer's Ballade of Good Counsel

Geoffrey Chaucer's short poem "Truth," also known by its French title *Balade de Bon Conseyl*, confronts one of the enduring moral questions of human existence: how can a person live virtuously in a world so thoroughly marked by corruption, instability, and false ambition? Rather than offering an abstract philosophical argument, Chaucer approaches this problem through a series of proverbial injunctions—compact, memorable pieces of practical wisdom that together sketch a way of life grounded in moral integrity. The poem urges its reader toward self-restraint, warning against the dangers of striving too eagerly after worldly gain. It counsels contentment with what one has, suggesting that the endless pursuit of more only entangles the soul in anxiety and disappointment. Above all, it advocates a spiritual detachment from earthly ambition, encouraging the reader to release his grip on the fleeting rewards of fortune and status.

These moral exhortations reflect a deeply medieval understanding of the relationship between the temporal and the eternal. The world, in Chaucer's vision, is a place of "wrastling," a scene of struggle and precariousness in which those who cling too tightly to material success are bound to be disappointed. To flee from the crowd, to be satisfied with modest circumstances, and to govern one's own conduct rather than seeking to command others—these are the practical foundations of the virtuous life the poem describes. In this way, the individual voice of the poem becomes a guide, addressing the reader directly and drawing him away from the delusions of the world toward a more secure and lasting good.

The heart of the poem lies in its refrain, "trouthe schal delyvere, hit is no drede"—truth shall deliver you, there is no doubt. This repeated affirmation carries the poem's central conviction: that fidelity to truth, and through it to God, will ultimately liberate the soul from bondage. The word "trouthe" here bears a rich medieval meaning, encompassing not only honesty and factual accuracy but also faithfulness, loyalty, and steadfast integrity in one's relationship to the divine. To hold fast to truth is thus to remain faithful to God, and such faithfulness carries the promise of deliverance—a release from the entrapments of the fallen world.

This vision of deliverance is inseparable from the poem's framing of earthly life as a spiritual pilgrimage. Chaucer reminds the reader that "here is non hoom, here nis but wildernesse"—this world is not our true home but merely a wilderness through which we journey. The image of the pilgrim, the "beste," urged to lift up his eyes and give thanks, transforms the whole of life into a passage toward a heavenly homeland. Earthly existence becomes not an end in itself but a road leading elsewhere, and the hardships and temptations along the way are understood as trials to be endured rather than treasures to be seized. In this light, the poem's counsel of detachment is not merely prudent advice but a preparation for the soul's final journey home.

Taken as a whole, "Truth" distills a profound spiritual teaching into a form both accessible and enduring. Its proverbial wisdom addresses the immediate difficulties of living well among the corruptions of the world, while its refrain lifts the reader's gaze beyond those difficulties toward an ultimate liberation. In binding together practical counsel and religious hope, Chaucer offers a poem that is at once a guide for daily conduct and a meditation on the deepest purpose of human life—the return of the faithful soul to its eternal home.

# Learning French: Does Effort Alone Suffice?

When it comes to mastering a new language, few fields are as rewarding—or as challenging—as **FLE** (*Français Langue Étrangère*, or French as a Foreign Language). Students around the world dedicate countless hours to grammar drills, vocabulary lists, and pronunciation exercises, all in pursuit of fluency.

## Motivation Is the Starting Point

Many learners wonder whether motivation and hard work alone **suffice** to reach a high level of proficiency. The honest answer is that determination is essential, but it rarely works in isolation. Passion opens the door, yet consistent practice and real exposure to the language are what carry you through.

## What You Really Need

To succeed **for** the long term, consider combining several key ingredients:

- **Immersion** – Surround yourself with authentic French through films, podcasts, and conversation.
- **Structure** – A well-designed FLE course provides the scaffolding your brain needs to build lasting knowledge.
- **Feedback** – Interacting with teachers or native speakers helps correct mistakes before they become habits.
- **Patience** – Language acquisition is a marathon, not a sprint.

## A Balanced Approach

No single method will **suffise** on its own. The most effective path blends formal instruction with everyday practice, allowing theory and real-world use to reinforce one another. Whether you are studying **for** travel, career advancement, or personal enrichment, remember that steady progress beats occasional intensity.

In the end, learning French through **FLE** is a journey best undertaken with curiosity, discipline, and the willingness to embrace mistakes as part of the process.

---

# Truth (Balade de Bon Conseyl)

by Geoffrey Chaucer

This is one of Chaucer's most famous short poems, offering moral and spiritual counsel. Here it is in Middle English:

---

**Truth**

Flee fro the prees, and dwelle with sothfastnesse,
Suffyce unto thy thing, though it be smal;
For hord hath hate, and climbing tikelnesse,
Prees hath envye, and wele blent overal;
Savour no more than thee bihove shal;
Reule wel thyself, that other folk canst rede;
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.

Tempest thee noght al croked to redresse,
In trust of hir that turneth as a bal:
Gret reste stant in litel besinesse;
And eek be war to sporne ayeyns an al;
Stryve noght, as doth the crokke with the wal.
Daunte thyself, that dauntest otheres dede;
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.

That thee is sent, receyve in buxumnesse,
The wrastling for this world axeth a fal.
Her is non hoom, her nis but wildernesse:
Forth, pilgrim, forth! Forth, beste, out of thy stal!
Know thy contree, look up, thank God of al;
Hold the heye wey, and lat thy gost thee lede:
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.

**Envoy**

Therfore, thou Vache, leve thyn old wrecchednesse;
Unto the world leve now to be thral;
Crye him mercy, that of his hy goodnesse
Made thee of noght, and in especial
Draw unto him, and pray in general
For thee, and eek for other, hevenlich mede;
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.

---

## A Few Notes on Meaning

The poem's central message is captured in its refrain: **"And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede"** ("And truth shall set you free, there is no doubt").

Key advice includes:
- **"Flee fro the prees"** — flee from the crowd/throng
- **"Reule wel thyself, that other folk canst rede"** — rule yourself well, you who advise others
- **"Forth, pilgrim, forth!"** — a reminder that earthly life is only a temporary journey

The envoy addresses a "Vache" (possibly Sir Philip de la Vache, a friend of Chaucer), urging him to turn away from worldly attachment and toward God.
